newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh opposition calls for national strike.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh opposition calls for national strike.

text.p: The main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) on Wednesday called for a countrywide general strike on Sunday in its first attempt to topple the eight-month-old government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina.
"We can't give them any more time. They have proved more than inefficient in running the country," BNP leader and former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia told a party rally in Dhaka.
She urged all nationalist forces to "observe a countrywide strike from dawn to 2 p.m. on March 23 to overthrow the inefficient, corrupt and anti-people government".
Sunday is a working day in mainly Moslem Bangladesh.
Khaleda branded Hasina's government "shamelessly pro-Indian", and said it had conspired to "let the big hegemonist power enhance its influence on the small neighbour".
"They (the government) have entered an unequal deal with India to share river water (from the Ganges) and are attempting to buy power from that country," Khaleda said.
"They have made secret deals allowing India to use Bangladesh territory (to reach insurgents in northeastern Indian states) and are planning to open Chittagong port for use by India.

"We can no longer cooperate with this government or keep silent when national interests are at stake," Khaleda told cheering supporters. "We will never allow the government to implement any of the agreements it has signed with its big brother (India)."
Khaleda also attacked Hasina's handling of the economy.
"The government has failed to deal with deteriorating law and order. The economy is in a shambles. Let us strike now, and strike hard."
Telecommunications Minister Mohammad Nasim expressed "shock and surprise" at the BNP's call for a strike.
"This is very abrupt and illogical... This will serve no purpose other than to cause suffering to the people.
"The call for hartal (strike) is a naked expression of BNP's political bankruptcy," Nasim told Reuters.

He dismissed the BNP's allegations, saying the ruling "Awami League was the initiator of the independence movement in 1971 and shed more blood than any other party had. So it would never sell out national interests to any country or power."
Nasim urged Bangladeshis not to be misled by the BNP's "selfish propaganda" and to reject the strike call.
Hasina took office last June after the Awami League defeated the BNP in general elections billed free and fair at home and abroad.
The BNP said the poll results were rigged in favour of the Awami League and previously has threatened to disrupt government.
Independent analysts on Wednesday said the BNP's action, if successful, would damage the country's economy.
"Investors will become hesitant, reforms will suffer and the people will be the ultimate losers," said Matiur Rahman Chowdhury, editor of the Banglabazar Patrika newspaper.
